title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media
authors: Robert Lipton, Prakash K. C.
abstract: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

infographic.key_insight: A frame-based nonlocal theory couples strain and fracture through constitutive softening to predict strength and crack evolution in brittle anisotropic materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports dynamic and quasi-static fracture prediction where material strength, fracture energy, and anisotropy influence failure.
method: Use a nonlocal deformation gradient for anisotropic stress analysis.
Couple a constitutive phase field with displacement evolution governed by Newton’s second law.
Embed scaled strength surfaces in constitutive laws to govern softening and fracture.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons with experiments and other simulations, including strength prediction in titania and dynamic crack branching in soda-lime glass and concrete.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify prediction errors or computational cost, leaving accuracy and scalability to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
authors: Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, Peng Chen
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

infographic.key_insight: A properly constructed first-order least-squares residual can reliably measure nonlinear PDE solution error in the equation’s natural norm near a solution branch.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For nonlinear solid mechanics, including compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, this supports surrogate training with an inference-time error indicator.
method: Establish residual–error equivalence using linearized stability and Lipschitz continuity of the residual derivative.
Train a reduced-basis neural operator in a conforming finite element space, using solution snapshots only to construct the basis.
Assemble the physics loss and its symbolically derived gradient with a finite element library.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show that square-root loss excess tracks error and that the operator outperforms grid-based baselines in the PDE-compliant norm when evaluated in the same finite element space.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on PDE-specific stability and regularity conditions and may hold only near a solution branch.
infographic.paper_title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation
authors: Qing Cheng, Yuqi Sun, Xuejun Xu
abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy produces constitutive degradation directly from a variational energy functional, without an independent fracture field or prescribed degradation law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation connects sharp-crack energetics to diffuse-crack simulation for dynamic fracture and impact problems.
method: Apply a bounded saturation potential to scaled, nonlocally averaged tensile energy while keeping compressive energy local.
Derive tensile stress degradation through the adjoint averaging operator acting on the potential derivative.
Use a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme with an exact discrete modified-energy–external-work balance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports classical elastic-energy recovery for fixed smooth, bounded-strain fields as the averaging radius vanishes, Griffith surface-energy recovery for planar openings, and SAV–velocity-Verlet comparisons in crack branching and Kalthoff–Winkler impact.
infographic.watch_item: The stated limiting results do not establish convergence for general evolving cracks, and the abstract gives no quantitative benchmark errors.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation

title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
authors: Stanislas Pamela, Nicolas Pailliez, Emmanuel Franck, Victor Michel-Dansac, Laurent Navoret, Vignesh Gopakumar
abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

infographic.key_insight: Fuse-PINN combines finite-element methods and physics-informed neural networks to enable scalable multi-GPU simulations of nonlinear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets large-domain nonlinear physics simulations on GPU-based HPC systems, with demonstrations relevant to magnetic confinement fusion rather than solid mechanics.
method: Formulates a finite-element method for neural networks (FEM-NN).
Uses a modular framework for parallel PINN computation across GPUs.
Applies Energy Natural Gradient Descent for high-precision convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports nonlinear convective demonstrations with fine-scale dynamics and near-perfect multi-GPU scaling as problem size increases.
infographic.watch_item: Increasing-problem-size scaling does not establish fixed-size speedup, and the abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or computational-cost comparisons.
infographic.paper_title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
authors: Yue Yu, Jihong Wang, Stewart Silling, Ziwei Yang
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

infographic.key_insight: Mesoscale neural operators learn nonlocal constitutive laws from molecular dynamics while preserving strain energy density and fracture energy across scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables continuum fracture predictions on domains much larger than the atomistic training specimens.
method: Learn a nonlocal kernel and nonlinear constitutive relation from MD loading and displacement data.
Normalize the kernel to preserve strain energy density under horizon rescaling.
Rescale critical bond stretch to maintain consistent energy release rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic tests recovered the nonlocal model; MD-based tests matched energy metrics within 3% and out-of-distribution peak forces within 6%, with fracture branching demonstrated on a plate 4000 times the training-specimen area.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the reported tests; transfer to other materials and loading regimes requires further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions

title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities
authors: Jeonghun J. Lee
abstract: We study distributed optimal control of a linear poroelastic system in a total pressure formulation, with displacement and fluid-pressure tracking and box constraints on the source control. A mechanical Schur complement gives well-posedness at zero storage for each fixed finite Lamé parameter, without estimates that grow like the inverse storage coefficient. We discretize the state and adjoint with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping, and use piecewise constant controls. Under the stated regularity assumptions and a positive lower bound on storage, we prove first-order control and state error estimates uniform as the Lamé parameter increases. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, examine the dependence on the Lamé and storage coefficients, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.

infographic.key_insight: A total-pressure formulation enables locking-free poroelastic optimal control, with first-order discretization error bounds uniform as the Lamé parameter increases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports source-control optimization in nearly incompressible porous materials while tracking displacement and fluid pressure under box constraints.
method: Use a mechanical Schur complement to establish zero-storage well-posedness for each fixed finite Lamé parameter.
Discretize states and adjoints with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping.
Represent source controls as piecewise constants with box constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm predicted convergence rates, examine Lamé and storage coefficient dependence, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.
infographic.watch_item: The uniform first-order error estimates require the stated regularity assumptions and a positive storage lower bound; they do not establish zero-storage convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities

title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
authors: Erfan Hamdi, Joel Shor, Emma Lejeune
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs can generate correct finite element code, but reliable scientific automation requires consistency across attempts and independent verification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automating nonlinear mechanics and structural dynamics coding is promising, but passing self-generated checks does not establish numerical correctness.
method: Extend FEM-Bench to 17 nonlinear, history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics tasks.
Evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback.
Compare two execution-enabled agentic harnesses for six models and analyze 249 failed trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: An exploratory separate coder–tester configuration achieved the highest observed scores: 97.6% probability of at least one success in three attempts and 88.8% probability that all three succeed.
infographic.watch_item: Agentic gains varied and regressions occurred; in 28.5% of failed trajectories, tests shared an error with the implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis

title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity
authors: Ketan Mittal, Julian Andrej, John Camier, Veselin Dobrev, Tzanio Kolev, Leonardo Molinari
abstract: High-order mesh r-adaptivity typically entails minimizing a nonlinear functional using its gradients and, for Newton-based methods, its Hessian. These derivatives can be expensive to derive, must be updated with any changes to the functional, and errors in the derivatives directly impact the convergence of r-adaptivity. Additionally, derivatives of the r-adaptivity operator are required for consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse problems. This work develops a framework for differentiable r-adaptivity based on the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm. Given a pointwise functional defining the local mesh-adaptation objective, the proposed framework uses $\partial$FEM to automatically generate pointwise first- and second-order derivatives. These local derivatives are then assembled into a global gradient vector and a Hessian operator through the finite element operator decomposition. The derivative kernels support portable CPU and GPU execution, with partial assembly and tensor sum factorization enabling matrix-free application of the Hessian operator. The framework also provides consistent sensitivities of the r-adaptivity operator through automatically generated mixed derivatives and implicit differentiation of the mesh stationarity equations. Numerical experiments show GPU solve times comparable to those of hand-derived TMOP implementations on a benchmark problem, improvement in r-adaptivity convergence due to accurate computation of the derivatives, and demonstrate the use of mesh sensitivities for material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.

infographic.key_insight: Automatically generated derivatives enable differentiable high-order mesh r-adaptivity with accurate optimization gradients, Hessians, and mesh sensitivities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports adaptive finite element meshing and consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse engineering problems while reducing manual derivative development.
method: Define local mesh-quality objectives using the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm.
Use ∂FEM to generate pointwise first, second, and mixed derivatives, then assemble finite element operators.
Apply Hessians matrix-free on CPUs and GPUs and obtain mesh sensitivities by implicit differentiation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report GPU solve times comparable to hand-derived TMOP implementations on a benchmark, improved r-adaptivity convergence, and material-interface identification in inverse heat conduction.
infographic.watch_item: Consistent mesh sensitivities rely on sufficiently converged stationarity equations and a well-conditioned Hessian solve.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity

title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition
authors: Gung-Min Gie, Chang-Yeol Jung, Bongsuk Kwon, Kiwoong Kwon
abstract: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks defined on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all values of the network parameters, and the loss is the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual. We show that the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks, the boundary and convection terms carry no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during the training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

infographic.key_insight: SDGNN combines staggered discontinuous Galerkin structure with neural networks to bound solution error by discretization error, a computable loss-based training term, and network projection error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers an error-aware neural solver for scalar elliptic engineering models, including problems with prescribed interface jumps.
method: Patchwise networks satisfy SDG continuity conditions for every parameter choice.
Training minimizes the squared dual norm of the weak residual without differentiating the networks.
The formulation uses no boundary penalty or convection stabilization weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments show that square-root loss tracks error during training, prescribed square and circular interface jumps are captured consistently across initializations, and SDGNN outperforms PINNs at matched parameter counts.
infographic.watch_item: The loss controls the training-error component, not the full solution error; discretization and network projection errors must also be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition

title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision
authors: Abhijith Thoopul Anantharanga, Brandon Runnels
abstract: Spallation in ductile materials under high strain rates occurs through the process of void nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Void nucleation is known to depend on factors ranging from microstructural to stress state. The criteria for void nucleation in damage models are stochastic, and microstructural awareness is often neglected. Recently, it was shown that nucleation propensity can be estimated using computer vision. In the present work, this is integrated with a continuum damage model framework for comprehensive simulation of spallation in tantalum under plate impact. Void nucleation probability is governed by a susceptibility field, predicted from grain orientations and grain boundary (GB) energy, with a mechanical barrier set by the local maximum principal stress. This is coupled to a crystal plasticity model within a Lagrangian shock simulation, with microstructure selectively resolved to reduce computational cost. The model is calibrated at a flyer velocity of 196 m/s, where the simulated free surface velocity (FSV) matches experimental measurements of shock arrival, peak state, release and the pullback signal measured in flyer impact experiments, with some deviations confined to the late time ringing. With no further parameter changes, the model transfers to a 214 m/s case and accurately reproduces the FSV. To demonstrate the microstructure-awareness of the nucleation model, a selection of synthetic microstructures is presented for comparison. In the resolved microstructure, voids nucleate predominantly (though not exclusively) at GBs and triple junctions. It is shown that the FSV differs significantly based on the incorporated microstructure, yielding the correct FSV prediction only in the case of representative microstructures.

infographic.key_insight: Computer-vision-informed void nucleation makes shock damage predictions sensitive to grain-scale microstructure, with representative microstructures needed to reproduce measured free-surface velocity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports microstructure-aware prediction of spallation in tantalum under high-rate plate-impact loading.
method: Predict a void-nucleation susceptibility field from grain orientations and grain-boundary energy.
Combine susceptibility with a local maximum-principal-stress barrier in a continuum damage model.
Couple damage to crystal plasticity in a Lagrangian shock simulation with selectively resolved microstructure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calibrated at 196 m/s flyer velocity, the model reproduced key experimental free-surface-velocity features and transferred to 214 m/s without parameter changes, with some late-time ringing deviations.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the reported tantalum impact cases, and predictions depend on using representative microstructures.
infographic.paper_title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision

title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs
authors: Zijiang Yang, Xiaomeng Wu, Chen Kuang, Dongmei Fu
abstract: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ZijiangY1116/PANO.

infographic.key_insight: PANO combines interactions learned in parallel latent spaces to reduce information loss from compressing PDE observations into a single representation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports learned prediction of physical fields, including equivalent plastic strain in stamping, with potential value for solid-mechanics simulation surrogates.
method: Compress observations through independent mappings into parallel latent spaces with shared interaction parameters.
Use Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) for bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding.
Use Pairwise Latent Space Attention (PaLA) for adaptive cross-space updates, then fuse decoded results.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nine benchmarks covering diverse physics, geometries, and observation scales, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, including at least 28.3% lower equivalent-plastic-strain prediction error on Unilateral Stamping and 21.4% lower lift-coefficient prediction error on AirCraft versus existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify runtime or memory costs, so the computational overhead of parallel latent spaces needs assessment before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs

title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions
authors: Sharan Nurani Ramesh, Lea Saßmannshausen, Axel Klawonn, Daniel Balzani
abstract: This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries. The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport. Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization. A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction. Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections. Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa). This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch. A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries. Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.

infographic.key_insight: Simulations suggest calcium channel blockers reduce arterial media stress but shift load to the fibrous cap, potentially increasing plaque rupture risk when blood pressure reduction is insufficient.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupled drug-transport and arterial-mechanics modeling can reveal local stress trade-offs that smooth muscle relaxation alone does not capture.
method: Couple mechanical equilibrium with 3D reaction–diffusion drug transport.
Model calcium-dependent smooth muscle contraction, anisotropic tissue behavior, and residual stresses.
Fit material parameters to published experiments and run finite element simulations on histology-derived artery geometries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five geometries, fibrous cap stress increased with median increases up to 28.9 kPa; a 10 mmHg blood pressure reduction limited median increases to at most 3.8 kPa in four geometries.
infographic.watch_item: Results are morphology-dependent predictions from five exemplary geometries; the proposed rupture-risk implication requires experimental and clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Pharmaco-mechanical computational simulation of atherosclerotic arteries: effects of calcium channel blockers on local stress distributions

title: A Divergence-Free Finite Element Discretization of a Convection-Cooling Optimal Control Problem
authors: Tongxin Wang, Zhaojie Zhou
abstract: In this paper, we develop and analyze a finite element discretization for a bilinear optimal control problem governed by a stationary convection-diffusion equation, in which an incompressible velocity field acts as the control through the convective term. Continuous piecewise linear finite elements are employed to approximate the state and adjoint variables, while the Stokes-type optimality equation for the velocity control is discretized by a low-order, pointwise divergence-free ($P_1^c\oplus RT_0-P_0$) finite element. To accommodate the nonconforming velocity space, we construct a discrete cost functional by replacing the continuous $H^1$-seminorm regularization with a suitable discrete velocity bilinear form and derive the corresponding discrete first-order optimality system. Since the bilinear coupling between the velocity control and the state variable renders the underlying optimization problem nonconvex, we establish local strong convexity of the discrete reduced cost functional under a second-order sufficient optimality condition at an isolated strict local minimizer of the continuous problem. Furthermore, by exploiting a divergence-preserving interpolation operator, auxiliary state and adjoint error estimates, and a stability relation between the discrete reduced-gradient residual and the control error, we derive a priori error estimates for the state, adjoint state and velocity control. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the optimized incompressible velocity in redistributing the temperature field and to verify the predicted convergence rates.

infographic.key_insight: A pointwise divergence-free finite element discretization enables incompressible velocity optimization for convection cooling, with a priori error estimates for the state, adjoint, and control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports computational design of incompressible flows that redistribute temperature while preserving the divergence-free constraint.
method: Approximate temperature and adjoint variables with continuous piecewise linear finite elements.
Discretize the velocity-control optimality equation using the low-order P1c ⊕ RT0–P0 divergence-free element.
Use discrete velocity regularization and second-order optimality conditions to establish local strong convexity and error estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate temperature redistribution by the optimized velocity and verify predicted convergence rates; the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The optimization is nonconvex, and the analysis relies on a second-order sufficient condition at an isolated strict local minimizer rather than guaranteeing global optimality.
infographic.paper_title: A Divergence-Free Finite Element Discretization of a Convection-Cooling Optimal Control Problem

title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
authors: Vladimir A. Lazovskiy, Victor B. Kazantsev, Sergey V. Stasenko
abstract: We present the first complete implementation of $β$-reduction in the untyped $λ$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $θ$--$γ$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

infographic.key_insight: The authors report a fully spiking implementation of untyped lambda-calculus beta-reduction using biologically documented neural mechanisms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work suggests a route to symbolic computation on neuromorphic hardware, rather than a demonstrated application to solid mechanics or constitutive modeling.
method: Use leaky integrate-and-fire neurons to detect reducible expressions, segment subterms, and track variable bindings.
Implement index arithmetic, token copying, and role maintenance through phase dynamics, spike-timing-dependent plasticity, and persistent firing.
Derive synaptic weights analytically from measured excitatory postsynaptic potential amplitudes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 100% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church arithmetic, Boolean logic, Y-combinator steps, noise robustness, and determinism.
infographic.watch_item: The reported validation does not establish scalability, hardware efficiency, or applicability to solid-mechanics problems.
infographic.paper_title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms

title: Finite element nonlinear nudging for the Navier-Stokes equations
authors: Elizabeth Carlson, Rui Fang, Ali Pakzad
abstract: Nonlinear nudging augments the classical linear nudging (continuous data as- similation) term with a nonlinear feedback that strengthens as the observed error decreases, and yields super-exponential convergence to the true state. In this paper, we study nonlinear nudging for the 3-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with the finite element method, which allows complex geometries and physical boundary conditions. We propose an implicit-explicit (IMEX) finite element scheme with inf-sup stable elements, prove its unconditional long-time stability, and show for the spatially semi-discrete scheme that the error reaches a prescribed tolerance in finite time. Our analysis also suggests that the non- linear nudging term requires the mesh resolution to be fine enough (${χ= O(H^{-1})}$, where $χ$ is the nonlinear nudging intensity and ${H}$ is the observation mesh size). Further, our error estimates suggest that a larger nonlinear exponent $γ$ requires finer observational resolution, which is confirmed by numerical tests. Numerical experiments, including two-dimensional forced viscous flow in a periodic box, flow past a cylinder, and flow over a flat plate, show that nonlinear nudging synchronizes with the true solution considerably faster than linear nudging. We also show that observations in a subregion suffice to synchronize the whole flow

infographic.key_insight: Nonlinear nudging accelerates synchronization with the true Navier–Stokes flow by strengthening feedback as observation error decreases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Finite element implementation supports flow-state reconstruction in complex geometries with physical boundary conditions, including from observations confined to a subregion.
method: Augment classical linear nudging with nonlinear error feedback.
Use an implicit–explicit finite element scheme with inf-sup stable elements.
Prove unconditional long-time stability and finite-time attainment of a prescribed error tolerance for the spatially semi-discrete scheme.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests in a periodic box, past a cylinder, and over a flat plate show considerably faster synchronization than linear nudging and demonstrate whole-flow synchronization from subregion observations.
infographic.watch_item: Observation resolution must be sufficiently fine for the nonlinear intensity and exponent; the analysis suggests χ = O(H⁻¹), and larger γ requires finer observations.
infographic.paper_title: Finite element nonlinear nudging for the Navier-Stokes equations

title: Direct Element-Level Mass Matrix Inversion
authors: Eli Hanukah
abstract: Explicit finite element methods for transient solid dynamics commonly use lumped mass matrices to avoid solving systems of equations for nodal accelerations at each time step. However, diagonal mass matrices may inadequately represent inertia, particularly for higher-order elements and coarse or distorted meshes. This has limited the use of higher-order elements in explicit dynamic analyses. This paper presents a systematic method for directly evaluating the inverse of non-diagonal element-level mass matrices for solid isoparametric elements of arbitrary interpolation order. The method applies to mixed mass matrices defined as linear combinations of lumped and consistent mass matrices, with a weighting parameter controlling the transition between diagonal, consistent, and intermediate formulations. It therefore provides a framework for incorporating non-diagonal mass formulations, including those for quadratic elements, into explicit finite element algorithms. The approach is demonstrated by deriving an explicit inverse formula for the mixed mass matrix of the eight-node hexahedral element. This formula enables efficient element-level inversion without solving a global system. The proposed method can improve inertial representation in transient dynamic analyses while retaining the computational advantages of explicit time integration and is suitable for element-by-element implementations.

infographic.key_insight: Direct element-level inversion of non-diagonal mass matrices offers a path to richer inertial representation in explicit finite element dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support higher-order solid elements without requiring a global mass-matrix solve at each explicit time step.
method: Develop a systematic inversion method for solid isoparametric element mass matrices of arbitrary interpolation order.
Blend lumped and consistent mass matrices using a weighting parameter.
Derive an explicit inverse formula for the eight-node hexahedral element.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an analytical eight-node hexahedral demonstration, but no quantitative accuracy, stability, or runtime benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Element-level inverses do not automatically yield the inverse of the assembled global mass matrix; integration into an explicit solver requires care.
infographic.paper_title: Direct Element-Level Mass Matrix Inversion

title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
authors: Flavia Gehrig, Carolin Birk, Matti Schneider
abstract: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.

infographic.key_insight: A matrix-free FFT solver combines scaled boundary finite elements with a Fourier-space preconditioner to deliver stable voxel-based elastic homogenization without the excessive stiffness of fully integrated elements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports effective-property prediction for porous and highly heterogeneous materials while accommodating arbitrary stiffness anisotropy.
method: Discretize a regular periodic voxel grid with hexahedral SBFEM cells, using analytical radial solutions.
Apply a homogeneous SBFEM stiffness-based preconditioner locally in Fourier space.
Avoid global stiffness-matrix storage, with a preconditioned condition-number bound governed by material contrast rather than grid resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on a short-fibre composite, polyurethane foam, and a sand-based binder jet microstructure show robust convergence and competitive accuracy, including stability where reduced-integration elements become unstable.
infographic.watch_item: The stated condition-number bound depends on material contrast; grid-resolution independence alone does not guarantee contrast-independent convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics

title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture
authors: Varun Darshana Parekh, Anusha Devulapally, Sivani Devarapalli, Cassius Henderson, Shimeng Yu, Vijaykrishnan Narayanan
abstract: The drive toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages promises unmatched performance and customization, yet the resulting density amplifies thermal challenges. To facilitate rapid design space exploration, we present ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer-based, scale invariant surrogate that integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate to predict steady state temperature in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional finite element solvers such as ANSYS. To train the transformer model, we also create a dataset of 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures. On a 150 sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16°C and an MAE of 2.24°C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and by 71% over HotSpot, while running approximately 6x and 11x lower inference latencies respectively. Ablation studies confirm robust generalization to unseen floorplans. Code and dataset available at https://github.com/MicroSystemsDesignLab/ThermLeT

infographic.key_insight: ThermLeT predicts steady-state temperatures in 2.5D chiplet packages in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional FEM solvers such as ANSYS.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast thermal predictions can accelerate chiplet floorplan exploration and help engineers screen packaging designs for thermal risks.
method: Multimodal transformer integrates power density maps, spatial coordinates, material properties, and heat transfer rate.
Scale-invariant surrogate learns from 6,221 layouts perturbed from three representative architectures.
Predicts steady-state temperature fields without running a full FEM solve at inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 150 test samples, ThermLeT achieved 3.16°C RMSE and 2.24°C MAE, with reported accuracy improvements of 35% over ThermEDGe and 71% over HotSpot.
infographic.watch_item: Training layouts originate from only three architectures; performance on substantially different packages and operating conditions needs independent validation.
infographic.paper_title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture

title: Forests of Omnitrees: Analysis and Applications to Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements
authors: Nils Margenberg
abstract: We prove output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests, which bisect cells along selected axes. A canonical descriptor characterizes representable partitions independently of split order. Complete one-level cycles, including coarsening, face balance and selected coarse meshes, take sequential work proportional to stored input and output at fixed dimension and key width, with polynomial depth dependence even for unbalanced input. From balanced input, refinement-only balance stays within each request's coordinate slab; this bound is attained. Polynomial trace equations characterize conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions. Reconstruction moments bound interpolation errors and capture the logarithmic loss that bilinear nodal interpolation can suffer on balanced meshes. Elements of degree up to four resolve moving heat layers on unstructured 4D space-time and 5D space-time-parameter meshes. Multigrid uses the generated hierarchies.

infographic.key_insight: Omnitree forests enable axis-selective mesh adaptation with provably output-optimal work and a split-order-independent description of representable partitions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports anisotropic high-order finite elements and multigrid hierarchies for resolving moving layers in space–time and parameter-dependent simulations.
method: Represent partitions canonically, independently of cell-splitting order.
Prove work bounds for refinement, coarsening, face balancing and selected coarse-mesh construction.
Use polynomial trace equations for conformity and reconstruction moments for interpolation-error bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical complexity and approximation results, plus moving heat-layer resolution with polynomial degrees up to four on unstructured 4D space–time and 5D space–time–parameter meshes.
infographic.watch_item: Linear-work guarantees assume fixed dimension and key width; crossed-face conformity and logarithmic interpolation losses require care in implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Forests of Omnitrees: Analysis and Applications to Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements

title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy
authors: Bakhtiyar Mammadli, Karol Frydrych, Casim Yazici, Azad Mammadli, Kazimierz Skrobas, Siddharth Suman
abstract: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.

infographic.key_insight: PCA of full-field strain measurements reveals yielding signatures and early localized deformation associated with later failure in thermally exposed aluminum.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help identify plasticity onset and failure-prone regions that are difficult to distinguish in conventional strain maps.
method: Measure sequential strain fields using Digital Image Correlation during uniaxial tension.
Apply unsupervised Principal Component Analysis to extract temporal signatures and spatial deformation patterns.
Compare the second-component projection peak with 0.2% offset yield and inspect pre-transition component maps.
infographic.evidence_signal: For AA6063-T5 tested as received and after exposure to 100°C, 200°C, and 300°C, the second-component peak agreed with conventional yielding, while pre-transition PCA maps more clearly distinguished features associated with subsequent failure regions.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the reported alloy and loading conditions; robustness to measurement noise and broader material behavior remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy
